Revision 0: April 7, 2012 Place of Publication: India In the lotus of the heart, in the lotus of the navel, and likewise in the lotus of the mouth. (5)
The Supreme Self indeed dwells there; if you are able to know it, you should block the nine gates by restraining the nine channels.
Having withdrawn the nine winds, one should cause them to enter the heart-lotus;
the stalk of that lotus is indeed called the piṅgalā channel.
Thereafter, three principal channels, spoken of by her, are cast forth like clusters of gems upon a thread; having reached them, one should cause the city to be known.
Of these, indeed, there is one which is preeminent; by knowing that, the Supreme is known.
Within it resides that which is to be known—the imperishable cause of all.
Having understood this, O Mahāsena, you ought to perform what has been declared;
having resorted to the tenth door, the tenth nāḍikā flows.
Having attained the tenth wind, the equinox (viṣuvat) occurs;
one should cause that [wind] to grasp space gradually through the piercing of the knots.
Having indeed performed the union with Brahman and having correctly realized the supreme goal, he attains dissolution in the highest state, unwavering and perfectly concentrated. (12)
One should withdraw the self into the *praṇava*, having completely restrained the breath while pronouncing the *praṇava* adorned by the movement of the palate and the lips. (13)
Even one with a lifespan of an eon would thus proceed there without doubt;
all the instruments [of perception] and the knots of the gates are entirely dissolved.
Having understood that all the channels arise from the vital breath, one is liberated from everything;
as long as this is known, my son, so long does one remain absorbed in Brahman.
Having understood that, Mahāsena, you ought to perform the act of departure.
In what place does Brahmā abide, and by which door is he attained? O Lord, if you are pleased with me, please explain all of this.
Brahmā should effect the dissolution of Brahmā; from one being, he should perform the encircling within all beings. Otherwise, they will not succeed even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. (18)
"O God, having abandoned the elements, by what door does one attain perfection?
You ought to explain this entire doubt of mine to me in its entirety. (19)
O Six-faced One, that which you have asked is a secret more secret than the most secret, even a supreme secret; I shall tell you all of it.
The sun is situated in the midst of the sky; the moon is situated in the midst of the sun;
light is situated in the midst of the moon; and the Supreme is situated in the midst of light. 21.
Straight, smooth, and stainless,
like a streak of lightning yet difficult to behold, it is the heart of the sun and the moon, whose seat is the heart;
within them is the supreme radiance that does not abide in this world.
O Six-faced One, that mind which possesses great splendors is directly perceived;
indeed, behind the gate of Brahmā, this smoke stands on all sides. (24)
One should contemplate both that which resides in the heart and that which resides in the sky as one;
otherwise, O Śikhidhvaja, they will not be accomplished for those who lack this method.
That which I have described as the Supreme Brahman, established in the space of the heart—
that is Śakti, that is Śiva, knowledge, and the object of knowledge, the imperishable and immutable.
This is your union with Brahman; he who, through the gateway of Brahman, meditates upon Brahman, is instantly liberated from all sufferings.
At the time of his departure, this dissolution into Brahman is known to him;
indeed, O child, he is merged into the Supreme—such is the command of the Supreme Lord. (28)
One shall obtain the Brahman-vein, the Brahman-wind, and the [Brahman]...;
indeed, the Brahman should be contemplated as the imperishable syllable of Brahman. || 29 ||
The Praṇava is situated within the lotus of the heart; the Praṇava exists in the void as far as the realm of the cosmic egg, reaching down to Kālāgnirudra. (30)
O Śikhidhvaja, all this that consists of speech, as well as the entire three worlds with their moving and non-moving beings, has been seen by the Supreme through the Praṇava.
Everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass originates from the Praṇava;
those who speak of Brahman declare that one should effect its dissolution back into that very source.
He alone is the supreme state; He alone is the supreme imperishable. He is the three-syllabled [Om], divided threefold, abiding in three places, and consisting of the three qualities.
The triad of the three gods and the three fires is remembered as the supreme triad of deities;
[they worship] the god Śiva, the bearer of five forms, the supreme cause. (34)
Of the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas... || 35 ||
The Praṇava is the source and the place of dissolution for all;
therein indeed reside Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva himself. (36)
Indeed, the perfected ones were produced by the *praṇava*, and by the *praṇava* [itself];
it is both the imperishable and the perishable, the name and that which is devoid of name. (37)
That which is formless form is recited as the Praṇava;
it is both to be uttered and unutterable, and likewise both with sound and without sound.
He who upholds the supreme power bears both sound and the soundless, the sacred syllable *praṇava*,
as well as both mantra and non-mantra, and that which is graspable and ungraspable.
The *praṇava* exists everywhere through the distinction between the grasped and the grasper;
he who does not know the *praṇava* does not know the supreme abode of the universe. (40)
O child, how could there be liberation for him even in hundreds of millions of aeons?
Even today, a great doubt remains in my heart.
O Lord, tell me: in what place does Brahmā reside?
The illustrious Lord said: Brahmā, who sustains the bodies of living beings, is present everywhere;
moreover, my child, he is especially established in three locations.
In the lotus of the heart, in the lotus of the navel, and likewise in the lotus of the mouth,
that Lord is indeed perceived directly, abiding in a state of transformation.
It laughs and weeps, dances and likewise sings;
it eats and smells—listen, and I shall explain the cause thereof.
In opening and closing the eyes, in dejection and in joy, he experiences pleasure and pain, as well as the sensations of cold and heat. (5)
Hunger, thirst, sexual desire, sleep, awakening, and remaining awake—
these, O Six-faced One, are indeed perceived directly by him.
Neither another lamp nor the Supreme Self can be perceived by means of its own form.
(5) O Mahādeva, my wonder does not cease even now;
O Lord, I truly desire to hear about the God who resides in the three places.
I am pleased today, O son, that you have questioned me;
listen now to that Brahman abiding in three places, according to its sequence.
O Guha, he dwells eternally in the heart-lotus with a steady disposition;
he moves back and forth within the lotus of the mouth and the lotus of the navel.
The petals of the heart-lotus are proclaimed to be those very channels (nāḍīs);
all the vital breaths, beginning with prāṇa, flow within those channels.
Indeed, ten channels (nāḍīs) are proclaimed, and there are indeed ten winds;
the principal one is Piṅgalā, which is void, and it creates during the watch of the day.
It is situated at the navel of the entire wheel of channels;
likewise, Piṅgalā arises from the center of that very wheel of channels. (13)
Iḍā, Suṣumṇā, and Piṅgalā as the third—
though they are all a single body, their application is distinct in each case.
The *iḍā* flows on the left; there Soma is established. The *suṣumnā* and *piṅgalā* are on the right side; there the Sun is established. (15)
The Suṣumṇā is the central channel; everything always resides therein.
O God, that which is situated within the Iḍā is called the Pitṛyāna.
O son, that which is situated in Piṅgalā is called Devayāna;
Suṣumṇā is the central channel (madhyamā-nāḍī), and that which resides therein is the state of the path to liberation. || 17 ||
With every effort, the lord of yogis, who brings one to the stages of the path of liberation, [perceives] the unmanifest God, devoid of form, situated within the pericarp. 18.
All thirteen channels are pervaded by the constituent parts of that [central channel];
indeed, among them, one is heard of as being named Suṣumṇā. (19)
By her, three lotuses were spoken of as being like jewels strung on a thread;
within them, the prāṇa and apāna breaths are established, closely joined together.
O Śikhidhvaja, O Kumāraka, the prāṇa and apāna breaths, situated within the suṣumṇā,
abide in the form of creation and dissolution.
Bound by the supreme power (parā-śakti), which is unmanifest and like unto death,
they exist through the relationship of support and supported, distinguished as the higher and the lower.
Prāṇa and apāna are established in the form of creation and dissolution;
situated between them is Brahman, unmanifest and devoid of form.
He indeed swallows and creates the entire universe, both moving and unmoving;
the heart-lotus, however, is situated below the back of the navel-lotus and faces downward.
O son, having observed that supreme [point] between the two whorls (karṇikā), || 25 ||
"O Father, how may that range of form be seen by me, having seen which I shall go to the unborn, imperishable state? (26)
Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom, Lord of the Lords of Yoga! This question which you have raised is difficult to understand even for the gods.
Neither by Brahmā, nor by Sūrya, nor by Candra, nor by Viṣṇu,
nor even by the Goddess or by you has that which has been asked here been [previously] inquired after.
I shall indeed tell you that which is more secret than the secret, the supreme [teaching];
one should guard the speech of distraction like a protector of those who have sought refuge. (29)
The king's minister is to be well-guarded; he must not be given to just anyone.
He should not be given to one who is uninitiated, nor to one who is untrustworthy or dishonest. 30.
One should cause [the substance] to be given to one who is agitated, cruel-hearted, or wicked;
however, O son, it must be given to one who is initiated and who worships the Guru, the gods, and the fire.
To one who is faithful, has conquered anger, and is turned away from greed and delusion,
the teacher indeed examines the disciple for twelve years.
By this, the entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving, has been permeated.
Today my birth has become fruitful; today my learning has become fruitful;
today my intellect has become fruitful; today my austerity has become fruitful.
"O dear one, I have indeed accomplished my purpose; today I am truly born again.
And today, O father, I am indeed liberated from the bonds of worldly existence. (35)
O Lord, having understood the secret gnosis, I am forever satisfied;
now I wish to hear how the prāṇa and apāna are situated.
Listen, O dear child of great wisdom, to that which I have been urged by you;
I shall now explain to you how the prāṇa and apāna breaths abide.
The five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa, are situated in the upper part [of the body];
among them, two are proclaimed as the primary ones: prāṇa and apāna. (3)
Relying on the analogy of a ball, it moves downward and upward;
this same movement proceeds throughout all the paths of yoga.
Among the nine winds, prāṇa and apāna are proclaimed to reside in the heart-lotus, the navel-lotus, and likewise at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta).
The Supreme Self indeed enters, established in the movement of the prāṇa and apāna;
the apāna withdraws the prāṇa, and likewise the prāṇa [withdraws] the apāna.
Established in them, he creates and withdraws them;
for this is merely the rising and setting [of the mind], O Śikhidhvaja—I consider it nothing else.
For the sun situated externally, there is indeed neither rising nor setting;
it shines constantly, my child, illuminating the universe and the paths of the directions.
Therefore, with every effort, one should investigate that which resides within the body;
by knowing which liberation is attained, and through which one is not born again. || 9 ||
O Lord, I desire to know how the rising and setting [of the sun] occurs,
how day and night were established, and likewise the two types of transits (saṅkrānti).
"O son, though you are very dear to me, you ask an excellent question, my child; since you have posed this question which is beyond description, I shall tell it to you. (11)
O Six-faced One, that Supreme Brahman which I have described as residing in the heart— this [power] is its capacity with respect to its rising and setting.
When the flame of that radiance exists upon the upward path,
know that to be its arising— the signless appearing in the form of a sign, the unmanifest coming within the range of the manifest. (9)
O child, space itself would come into being for one who has indeed attained dissolution through power;
[so too] earth, water, fire, air, and space itself.
For these five great elements, from which they have arisen, indeed dissolve back into that [source];
it is as if the power of space devours the entire world, having itself been unswallowed.
O Guha, impelled by the command of Śiva, she indeed effects the creation;
O son, I have told you this dissolution of all beings.
And this was previously told to me by Śiva when he was always pleased:
"The origin and dissolution of beings have been understood by me in their various divisions;
I desire to know them further..."
[The form] established in Brahman, [having the appearance of] Brahmā. || 1 ||
O Guha, that most secret question which has been posed by you, I shall explain all of it; listen accordingly with focused attention.
Empty, empty again, empty; empty, empty again and again.
The empty that is emptier than the empty—that empty is indeed only empty. (3)
"‘Empty, empty’ has been proclaimed by you; through this, knowledge has arisen in me.
O Lord, if you are pleased with me, tell me of the non-emptiness of that which is empty. (4)
He who knows "empty, empty," and he who becomes "empty, empty"—one should recognize him as non-empty; for the dissolution of all emptiness is beneficial.
O child, that triple-void (triśūnya) resides within the hearts of all beings;
yet they do not know that void, by which they have been rendered non-void.
Śiva is to be known as having become void, for the powers (śaktis) have indeed become void.
Among those, this non-empty form is all-pervading and consists of consciousness. || 7 ||
For emptiness does not possess the state of being empty; its cultivation is emptiness itself.
Consciousness is the knower, empty, and supported by that which is without support.
Those of wise intellect say that the Void which exists through its sovereign power and by which this world is not filled—that Void they call "the Void. (9)
For that which is empty, emptiness does not exist; that which is non-empty is called empty.
Having transcended both creation and dissolution, the wise know the non-emptiness of the empty.
From the empty, creation proceeds; into the empty, moreover, dissolution occurs.
Therefore, non-emptiness within the empty is a support for that which is without support. 11.
The state of being supported by that which is without support is emptiness, by which it is established;
through the yoga of consciousness and primordial wisdom, you shall attain the knowledge of the empty object of cognition. 12.
Emptiness and non-emptiness are to be known; for emptiness does not exist anywhere at all.
This emptiness of theirs is empty for those in whom there is meditation upon it out of ignorance. (13)
"O child, the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, are never empty;
everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass is filled with the Void. (14)
That void was filled by Śakti, who is unmanifest and arises from Śiva;
just as the three worlds are awakened by the nature of consciousness. 15.
An entity is empty, yet that [emptiness] is not [mere] emptiness; emptiness is the emptiness of ignorance.
That emptiness is to be known through the form of gnosis; that emptiness is not [found] in the cave of the heart.
The emptiness of the knowable is the non-apprehension [of it], which is the realization of the absence of an objective support;
however, O son, there is no state of being empty within that which is empty in reality.
O Śikhidhvaja, formerly the entire world was shrouded in darkness;
the sun and moon had perished, along with the winds, planets, lunar mansions, and stars.
It is beyond reasoning and unknowable in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
it is neither above nor in the netherworld, and it is devoid of the great elements.
At that time, when manifestation is not seen and the unmanifest remains everywhere, Śiva arises through that power which has the nature of consciousness. || 20 ||
Having brought about dissolution in the state of Turiya, he indeed rained down abundant nectar;
for the sake of the welfare of the creation of beings, the entire world was inundated.
Then indeed the egg was produced, eight-limbed and resembling gold; until the end of the kalpa, that egg remained established in a subtle form. || 22 ||
But he, O dear one, having divided himself twofold, fashioned heaven and earth;
the eight directions, the eight intermediate points, and in the center, the seed-sprout as the foundational station.

This world, which has arisen through the power of consciousness (cicchakti) and is not bound [by material causes], rests upon the back of that sprout; there, indeed, is a great white and auspicious lotus.
One should recognize that syllable Om as a lotus, rich with a thousand petals and endowed with a pericarp and filaments; for a moment, one should contemplate it upon the lotus-petals.
O child, in its center arose Guha, a treasure-house of the Vedas;
O dear one, the Grandfather of all the worlds was situated at the end of the pericarp.
Then, O child, Maheśvara, the Lord of All and the creator of the universe, creates all beings, both moving and non-moving, as Prajāpati.
The Lord has four faces and four arms; he is the treasure-house of the four Vedas, resembling ten million suns and possessing a radiance like the fire at the end of an aeon.
By that radiance of splendor, the three worlds were illuminated;
at that moment, O dear one, the eight directions, the sky, and the earth became clearly manifest. (29)
O Six-faced One, the lotus situated upon the earth has Meru as its pericarp,
and its eight petals are the eight directions of the Brahma-lotus.
O child, the fourteenfold creation of beings, both moving and unmoving, all originates from the Praṇava; it arises through the power of consciousness and is born of sentience.
O child, [the universe] from Kālāgnirudra downwards arises as a sprout from the power of consciousness (cicchakti);
and that resides within the lotus, situated in the midst of the ocean of nectar.
Upon seeing him, Brahmā himself was struck with wonder in his inner self;
then, his mind became intent upon practicing yoga.
By him, yoga was practiced for ten thousand divine years;
through the power of consciousness, the attainment of the fruit of that yoga was withdrawn into the *praṇava*.
By him indeed was all this universe brought forth, including everything mobile and immobile,
from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, as far as the range of time and other categories.
Therefore, O Guha, all beings have become possessed of form and are composed of Brahman;
indeed, all this is Brahman, for one who speaks of Brahman knows the true meaning of "thou art That."
O child, those who, having known what is beneficial for all beings, remain steadfast, are indeed beyond rebirth;
they uphold the *praṇava*, the womb-power of all beings.

Therefore, from that which is born of Brahman, first within the wombs of the *praṇava*, by means of the *praṇava* there arises a lotus resembling the sprout of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). (38)
From the center of that, the Lotus-born (Brahmā) arose;
that is what is called the Praṇava, adorned with the Bindu, Nāda, and the Moon. || 39 ||
Joined with a full measure and a half-measure, by that means the knowers of Brahman understand it;
O Guha, the Praṇava is always born from the half-measure.
But one should effect dissolution into that very eternal Supreme Brahman which abides within the end of the sound (nāda); by this means, they are called exponents of Brahman (brahmavādinaḥ). 41.
O Supreme Brahman, whose banner is the flame arising from within Śiva;
by them the nectar has been known, and for them ignorance shall become poison.
Half a mātrā is a khavaṃśa; a part of that is a koṭiraṃśaka;
and even a hundred-thousandth part of that—one who knows this is a knower of Brahman. (43)
(23b) O Brahmāṇḍa, the origin of Brahmā has been known by me and heard by me;
now I wish to hear about the birth of both woman and man.
That question which you have raised is difficult to understand even for the gods;
I shall explain that secret to you here, following upon your inquiry.
Yoga was previously practiced by the Lotus-born One for the sake of creation,
and he performed a most great penance that was difficult to accomplish and wonderful to behold.
Then the Blessed Lord Śiva, the supreme cause, was pleased;
he is to be known as the supreme Brahman, Śiva, the highest state free from all affliction. || 4 ||
O child, Guha, the supreme and subordinate Śiva stands beyond all; by that God, when pleased, consciousness is bestowed through the power of consciousness (cicchakti).
"Go to the presence of Brahmā for the purpose of creating the creation;
for I was propitiated by him with supreme devotion. (6)
O God, O All-pervading Lord, how is it that You, who are perceptible, have been impelled by the power of consciousness?
From that time onwards, this lotus-bodied one has appeared before us in such a manner.
Thinking thus, one should know that all power exists in the form of Śakti; indeed, Viṣṇu himself, having assumed the form of power, abides as Śakti.
But I am the personification of Śiva himself, born from his splendor;
with both of us acting as seeds, the lotus-born Brahmā is the third.
Thus, O Guha, the threefold creation has arisen from that which is both existent and non-existent;
this indeed becomes the Praṇava, joined with the syllables A, U, and M.
Indeed, Nāda, Indu, Bindu, and Retas, as well as the Kalās and Mātrās,
constitute the twenty-four principles (tattvas), while Puruṣa is the twenty-fifth.
Life-span, karma, wealth, knowledge, and death itself, as well as whatever other bodily constituents there may be, whether manifest or unmanifest. || 12 ||
O Guha, when everything has become of one equal flavor through the unmanifest power of consciousness, they call that flavor "Brahman," the supreme source of bliss. (13)
One should know that seed to be immortality for mortals;
it is established as immortality for humans in the form of creation. || 14 ||
The immortality of the gods was ordained by him alone in the past,
as well as the fourteenfold creation of beings, both moving and unmoving, according to the rules.
O Guha, at the beginning, everything was of the nature of the bird (the Sun) created by Brahmā and the other gods;
O Śikhidhvaja, Agni and Soma were produced from the splendor of Brahman.
In this way, the seed-nature of a seed exists; otherwise, it would be meaningless.
Likewise, all undertakings are established within all seeds. (17)
For the purpose of creating the body, [the Self] is conscious by nature through the power of consciousness (cicchakti),
just as the Nyagrodha tree exists within the seeds of the Nyagrodha.

p. 25a) Likewise, I have learned from you the placement of creation (*sṛṣṭinyāsa*) pertaining to all beings, which resides within the mind through the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), as well as that which is divine and human. Furthermore, I ask again how the birth of a woman and a man occurs.
This is a secret, a great secret, the secret among all secrets;
hear all that you have asked as a question, O Six-faced One.
Due to remnants of past karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
beings are born within the cycle of existence across hundreds of thousands of different wombs.
The doer of good is born in a good womb, and the doer of evil among those who do evil;
thus, according to their actions, the doer indeed experiences what is auspicious or inauspicious.
When Yama and she both exist, and when emanation proceeds,
from the union of those two, through the meeting of the vulva and the phallus— (5).
Impelled by the power of consciousness, the embryo is conceived within the womb by the power [of the seed];
O Guha, the navel-lotus is situated behind the opening of the birth canal.
When the [vagina] of women has blossomed, that is the time;
for in this state, the menstrual flow (rajas) occurs for sixteen days.
But during the period of menstruation, O Śikhidhvaja, that lotus has its opening turned toward the downward path;
when the seed is cast into it at that time of menstruation— 8.
Then that seed grows; otherwise, it is devoid of form. Through the excellence of the man, there is excellence for the man; through the excellence of the woman, there is excellence for the woman.
When [the lunar days] are equal, it should be known as neuter; when there is an excess, it is nothing at all.
When they are even, it is male; when they are uneven, it is female; and by the time of the end, it is neuter.
For when the period of the season has passed, the lotus becomes full once again;
situated in its center, O child, is she born from the essence of Piṅgalā. (11)
O Śikhidhvaja, she brings joy to everyone at the time of sexual union;
likewise, the man always brings her joy. (12)
Then, through the union of both, the seed germinates;
for this indeed is the entry into the city and the attainment of immortality. || 13 ||
Then, without a doubt, sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons—the living beings who constitute the lineage—shall attain immortality. (14)
In the center of that lotus, O child, the power of consciousness (cicchakti), born of nectar,
dwells eternally for sixteen days.
Then the seed fallen from the *liṅga* sprouts in that very place;
this womb of the lotus, O Śikhidhvaja, is the bed of the embryo. (16)
O Guha, the Padminī [lotus] exists in the form of a conch as the bed of the womb;
one should imagine whatever is cast into its center as being like a seed.
Otherwise, however, this would be like medicine thrown upon that which has no seed.
"O Lord, everything has been known by me; O Father, everything has been heard by me.
Now I wish to hear about the origin of passion and semen."
O son, that which you have asked is extremely despicable; indeed, dwelling in the womb is proclaimed to be the lot of all evildoers. (2)
O Guha, everything within the scope of the cosmic egg, extending as far as Kālāgnirudra, is pervaded by the power of consciousness (cicchakti) and impelled by the command of Śiva.
All beings, flooded with the power of consciousness (cicchakti), abide within all things;
therefore, bring about growth and increase, otherwise there would be a contradiction of that [scriptural] injunction.
The manifest is not seen because of its unmanifest nature; yet that [unmanifest] creates. It produces the seed of that [manifest], and by it the moving and unmoving world is created. (5)
O Śikhivāhana, that which is the source and the end of all beings, both moving and unmoving— that, they know, is the ultimate reality.
But that should be known as the ultimate reality for which power is not lost;
and its power is not lost through union with Śiva, O Śikhidhvaja.
The Supreme Lord enters the womb of all beings— whether born from an egg, sweat, or a sprout— as well as fire, moon, and wind.
O Guha, this birth of living beings occurs through the rising of the prāṇa and apāna breaths; when these have subsided, there is death in every body, [yet] the Lord of the Body remains.
In the beginning, the elements were produced; afterwards, the cosmic egg came into being.
From that [egg] arose the sprout and the lotus, and immediately after that, Brahmā.
O Guha, the twenty-four principles are indeed indestructible;
from them, O Mahādeva, the Gāyatrī has emerged.
The entire universe, endowed with the pair of actions, has not emerged from them at all;
rather, everything within the interior of the cosmic egg originates from the power of consciousness (cicchakti). (12)
Therefore, my child, in the ultimate sense, the power of consciousness (cicchakti) always exists;
by me has the entire world been created—the creation of beings, both moving and unmoving. (13)
In the first month, the female *rajas* and male *retas*, mixed together, form a *kalila*;
in the second month, through the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), consciousness arises and it becomes a bubble (*budbuda*).
O Six-faced One, in the third month, [the embryo] arises from the union of semen and blood;
for it is from the power of consciousness (cicchakti) that all beings originate and remain within. || 15 ||
The conscious beings [perceive] the activity of the sprouting of all [beings], yet its manifestation is not seen because it is unmanifest; thus, he creates.
O Śikhivāhana, he beheld the end of that seed and sprout, as well as all moving and unmoving beings— both the mobile and the immobile creatures.
The power of consciousness (cicchakti), merged within the bubble and the sprout, produces the sprout; that stalk is proclaimed to be the navel-stalk of the lotus-womb. (18)
Then, O six-faced one, in the third month the formation of flesh and bone occurs;
just as a sprout from a seed, my child, it is unmanifest and not seen at all.
When the fourth month has arrived, the sprouts of the limbs are produced;
then the body becomes manifest, designated by the form of a person.
Through the power of consciousness (cicchakti), there arise within him only slight amounts of marrow, bone, sinew, fat, flesh, and blood. (21)
Wind, bile, and phlegm; semen, urine, and excrement;
veins, channels, and glands; orifices, valves, and networks—(22)
The skin, the vital points (marmas), the joints, the body hairs, and the channels—these and whatever others there may be that are causes for the production of the body. (23)
Indeed, all the limbs and members [of the body] come into being;
however, in the fifth month, neither body hair nor movement occurs. (24)
The ear and the conch-shell are the restoration of the elements for those whose elements have been impaired;
indeed, the manifestation of all limbs occurs exactly as it has been ordained for each.

O Śikhidhvaja, when you reached the sixth month, those [limbs] were endowed with the power of consciousness through the force of volition, as all the nutrients [derived] from your mother’s food [reached them]. 26.
Hunger, thirst, waking, sleep, cold, heat, pleasure, and pain—none of these perceive consciousness for the sake of the conscious being; rather, it is that which perceives consciousness itself.
When the seventh month has arrived, O Guha, the fire situated within the body awakens to a consciousness similar to that of humans.
Then he illuminates everything entirely within the body;
indeed, the three lotuses situated facing the navel awaken.
The vital winds, beginning with prāṇa, which have been proclaimed, as well as all the channels such as liṅginī and others, originate from the petals of the heart-lotus. (30)
All this is filled with the essence of fire by means of the fetal membranes;
O Six-faced One, the entire body is pervaded by them as far as the tips of the hairs.
Indeed, the entire network of channels is pervaded by all the rays,
just as at sunrise the whole world is pervaded by the sun's rays.
O Śikhidhvaja, having discerned the fire of life and the sun as pervading the body of the self,
one should direct the conscious power toward the object of consciousness outside, [as if] toward the sun.
But its own power of self-awareness does not perish as long as the power of consciousness is impelled;
however, by the eighth month, the intellect of the embryo comes into being.
Just as it is through the fault of egoism that I dwell in the womb—a place dense with blinding darkness and filled with every kind of suffering. (35)
In this place filled with sweat, urine, and excrement, mixed with fat and blood, defiled by phlegm and pus, and crowded with flesh, bones, and sinews; (36)
Of those twenty-one hells said to be terrifying,
the most formidable among them is the hell born from the womb.
Devoid of moon and sun, terrifying, and utterly lacking wind and fire, it resembles the ocean of hell, unbearable with its waves of suffering. (38)
"How was I born, O son? What evil deed have I committed?"—thus he reflected, impelled by the power of consciousness (cicchakti). || 39 ||
O Sage, when the time of the ninth month has arrived, those who dwell in the womb for longer than that [are rare]. 40.
Those who are great sinners and those who are secondary sinners—
on the tenth month, one should contemplate their vision and their meritorious deeds.
I shall do that by which I will cross over from the terrifying gateway of birth, and by which I shall not be born again. (42)
For indeed, all the meritorious deeds that have been described without exception in the Vedas, in all the Śāstras, in the Purāṇas, and in the Smṛtis— [43]
"I shall perform all those [deeds] exactly as described, according to the prescribed rules.
Having reflected thus, the birth was brought about by the power of consciousness (cicchakti) of the Manas. (44)
O Śikhidhvaja, the birth of the embryo is indeed a great terror;
O Guha, Maṇḍa is utterly terrified and agitated by it.
O Śikhivāhana, having torn open the lotus with his own hands, feet, and body, he entered the opening of the womb at the mouth of the embryo.
Then his mother, having reached the state of mortal fear, split open the womb through the opening and caused doubt for the mother. (47)
Having emerged, he falls to the ground and then becomes unconscious;
at that time, his mind is directed neither toward his own good deeds nor toward his evil actions.
Deluded by Māyā, O child, through the power of consciousness known as "childhood," this birth of living beings born from a womb has come to be, O Śikhidhvaja.
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice the state of the unborn.
"O Lord, there is nothing at all that has not been understood by me;
yet even regarding that, O Lord, doubt persists due to the exhaustion of my vital constituents. (1)
I shall answer this question which you have raised out of affection for your son—a question that is exceedingly profound, beyond direct perception, and outside the range of ordinary experience. (2)
Listen now to the enumeration of the elements and the limbs of this physical body, which is composed of the five gross elements and fashioned by the power of consciousness. || 3 ||

O child, for one satisfied by food containing the six tastes and whose bodily constituents (dhātus) are nourished, the [sexual] essence (rasa) is produced; however, for one month it remains fruitless.
That essence, by means of the power of consciousness (cicchakti), is indeed made into nectar in the form of rasa;
for that which arises from the supreme fire is truly not semen.
That should be known as the seed of creation; from it, creation proceeds. From the essence (rasa) comes blood, from that flesh, and from flesh fat is born.
From fat comes bone, and likewise from bone marrow; from marrow, semen is produced.
From semen arise all the bodily constituents (dhātus), and from these constituents arises the human body.
Their nourishment is satisfaction, while their expenditure is through the nourishment of the *rasas*;
for such, first of all, is the cause of the body's production. (8)
p. 31b) Furthermore, O dear one, listen to how it is:
wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (śleṣman) are proclaimed to be the constituent elements (dhātavaḥ). || 9 ||
Feces, urine, semen, marrow, and flesh is known as the eighth;
for these are the qualities that sustain the body, enumerated according to their number.
When the elements (dhātus) are in equilibrium within the body, all of them act as the producers of the qualities (guṇas). O Śikhivāhana, their number is this; such is the conceptualization.
O Guha, by the reversal of the elements, their number would not exist;
for whatever qualities are in the state of wind, those same are in fire, and likewise in sound.
But there is no equality among all elements for one who has passed beyond middle age; therefore, the elements of the past are immeasurable and inconceivable. (13)
O Śikhidhvaja, that fire which resides in the heart is indeed the meaning of the Praṇava; when it is fully gratified, O Guha, the bodily constituents (dhātus) are likewise gratified.
He indeed hears and he sees who tastes flavors for a long time;
remaining within the body, he experiences the qualities of smell and touch. (15)
Because of its existence, all those elements always dissolve;
therefore indeed, O child, it is at all times the cause of both the agent and the non-agent.
Just as thousands of rays are dependent upon the sun, O Six-faced One,
so too all beings are entirely dependent upon you.
I have understood the origin of the elements (dhātus) exactly and in great detail:
for all elements, blood comes first;
it exists in all embodied beings by depending upon the flesh. (2)
O child, his marrow shall be thirty-two palas in number;
his flesh shall be eight hundred and one peśīs. (3)
O Śikhidhvaja, having drunk milk, it becomes twice as much blood;
eight palas of bile, however, are situated together with phlegm and blood.
O Six-faced One, the phlegm is equal to the blood; its function is likewise.
Fat and marrow, however, exist separately, both weighing twenty palas each.
Semen and bile should be known as equal [in quantity] within the bones and marrow;
furthermore, from the consumption of food and drink, feces and urine are produced.
At that time, O Six-faced One, their states are indeed innumerable, and there is no stability whatsoever in them; [they consist of] blood, bile, phlegm, semen, and marrow.
These [tissues] arise from the rasa (nutritive fluid), yet they do not actually possess the nature of rasa itself;
for among all the bodily constituents (dhātus), pitta is indeed the cause of transformation, while śleṣman (kapha) is the binder.
Since all [beings] arise from the *rasa*, therefore that is their bond; since all [beings] arise from the *rasa*, therefore that is their bond. || 9 ||
In the marrow, however, there are twenty palas situated within all the bones;
as for the bones themselves, there are three hundred and sixty, with six more added.
Likewise, one should know that there are one hundred and eight sinews (tantrī), one hundred and eight layers of skin (carman), and exactly seven hundred veins (sirā). || 11 ||
And all those channels carrying blood remain covering the body;
furthermore, O child, there are one hundred and thirty-eight knots.
There are five principal knots by which the task is accomplished in the means to liberation;
and there is an innumerable network of sinews by which the cage of the body is bound. (13)
Flesh is indeed maintained by them, and those [tendons] are the effectors of contraction;
there would be sixty-four *kūrca*s, and from those two, the sinews (*snāyu*) arise. (14)
When it has been indicated that the sixty [joints] are bound together by cords of sinews, then this entire human body is seen to be composed of machinery. (15)
Seventy-two thousand channels have been proclaimed;
all of them carry the vital winds, and all of them are auspicious bestowers of liberation. (16)
Among them, one is preeminent, Piṅgalā, born from nectar;
all [the others] arise from her, just as the vital airs arise from the breath.
This single skin is renowned as being covered with hair on all sides;
the number of hairs is proclaimed to be thirty million or forty million.
And those channels have arisen from them because they originate from fire;
whether they be numerous or innumerable, they reside within the interior of the body.
All have arisen from splendor; all are established in splendor.
All the pores of the skin and all the gateways belong to Him whose vehicle is the peacock.
Due to ignorance they are not seen at all; they are seen by the eye of knowledge.
O Six-faced One, twenty nails and nine gates have been described. (21)
Thus has the enumeration arisen regarding the bodies of embodied beings.
I have heard from you the enumeration of the origin of all the constituent parts; now I desire to understand further the birth of the body from the abode of Brahman.
All questions have been answered by me, as well as all the secrets;
for this body is composed of Brahman, and it is here that Brahman is attained.
O Śikhidhvaja, I have previously explained the members [of the syllogism] in this way;
for if even one of them were absent, then all would indeed be purposeless.
These [elements], when combined, become the sustainers of the body;
yet each individual element likewise arises impelled by its own inherent power. (4)
But once again, that cage of elements is not at all constrained;
therefore, the entire human body is composed of machinery.
It resembles a householder's dwelling;
it is supported by bones, covered with skin, smeared with flesh and blood, and fastened together with nails of sinews. (6)
Indeed, the skin, smeared with its own coating and adorned with nine openings, supports that pillar by which the universe is sustained. (7)
The abode of Brahmā is always inhabited by his calf; in its center stands the Supreme.
It is in the middle of the abode of Brahmā and of the three sacred fires of the Veda.
The one who has maintained the sacred fires should perform their oblation every day with clarified butter,
fuel, sesame seeds, darbha grass, incense, perfumes, and auspicious garlands.
They derive neither satisfaction nor nourishment from those oblations known as "living beings";
rather, they are satisfied and satiated by the offerings of the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
For them, no oblation is offered that is lifeless or born of Brahman;
rather, O child, one should constantly offer the out-breath and in-breath, which arise from the immortal.
O child, the nectar situated in the fourth state flows continuously from the earth-receptacle toward the fire of the vital breath for its satisfaction.
By that [offering], the fires are satisfied; thus, the offerings of clarified butter are not in vain.
One should attend upon the external fires through rites prescribed by the rules.
The worlds Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar, along with Tapoloka, are seen by them as having all their offerings consumed;
this shall become the altar of Brahmā in the center of the abode of Brahmā.
Likewise, right here within this very space stands the Suṣumṇā at the inner altar (antarvedī);
as well as Prayāga, Kurukṣetra, Puṣkara, and Naimiṣa;
Vārāṇasī, the Gaṅgā, Kedāra, and the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean.
These and whatever other sacred fords and shrines there may be—
O Knower of Brahman, all abide in that supreme fire into which he offers oblations;
O Guha, everything exists manifestly established within all beings.
Out of ignorance they do not see at all; they see with the eye of knowledge.
Through your grace, I have heard about the abode of Brahmā as well as the clarified butter (ājya);
now I desire to hear about the Brahman residing within the city of Brahmā.
"O Guha, everything that you have asked has been explained by me;
yet this question must be learned with certainty from the mouth of a guru."
What secret is there in all the scriptures, including the Vedas and others, as well as in the Siddhānta and Kula-siddhānta, that is unspeakable to you? (3)

That which you have raised, O child, out of great affection—the eternally arisen and the eternal, as well as the impermanent which is of the nature of conceptual construction—I shall explain to you. (4)
O Śikhidhvaja, he who beholds that supreme splendor in the center of that lotus situated at the beginning, which arises from the Praṇava— he truly sees.
It was filled with great flames, surrounded by rays of light,
possessing an innumerable and radiant luster, illuminating the abode of Brahmā.
O son, he who perceives that is known by the knowers of Brahman;
because it resounds constantly, it is therefore called "Nāda" here.
O child, it abides as a continuous flow, just as rivers and reservoirs [flow];
that sound resounds uninterruptedly for all embodied beings.
Indeed, it is not different in each body; rather, it exists as one everywhere.
Some desire it to be non-luminous, while others declare it to be empty.
Some [say it is] a measure (mātrā), others a half-measure; the nihilists say "it does not exist, it does not exist.
O Guha, for those to whom that Nāda is manifest, liberation is certain. (10)
Through the various classifications of the *dhūlis*, that auspicious [knowledge] is perfected; it is perfected from the mouth of the Guru.
Having known you as Mahāsena, you will certainly attain liberation.
"O child, it must certainly exist; it abides in the form of the eternal (dhruva).
Guha, he utters that sound which has arisen from the supreme fire."
He reveals that reality; he is the Guru and indeed the Great Guru. He is to be known as the Instructor (Daiśika), for he is liberation itself and the one who bestows liberation. || 13 ||
Listen to the definition of sound so that you may perceive it as it truly is;
by the mere knowledge of which, deluded cognition ceases. (14)
O Guha, this sound is heard like that of a fire blazing in fuel, like water falling without agitation, or like a tree struck by the wind.
Likewise, O Six-faced One, hear this direct perception of the Brahman-body:
he who indeed hears it resounding with the roar of the sound of a horn. (16)
They call that sound "Brahman"; he who hears it truly hears.
O child, there is nothing whatsoever for him for whom that [sound] does not abide within.
But the deluded, deprived of both knowledge and realization, do not know it;
he alone sees and hears it clearly with the eyes of wisdom.
O Guha, one should block both ears with the tips of the index fingers;
by this means, the sound born of Brahman is heard, not the sound of teeth.
Thus indeed is the supreme Nāda situated in the hearts of all embodied beings;
for whatever forms exist, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, [they arise from it].
O child, that which resides in their hearts is obtained from the mouth of the Guru;
for this is accessible through the Guru’s instruction, provided he is pleased and speaks it. (21)
Otherwise, it would not be accomplished even in hundreds of millions of kalpas;
he is truly satisfied, he is indeed liberated, and he certainly partakes of the nectar of immortality.
O child, he for whom this Brahman is known—successively transmitted from one to another, handed down through tradition, higher than the highest, and beneficial—is truly wise. (23)
And that sound is fully described as that by which the moving and the non-moving—Brahmā and all beings, both mobile and immobile—is pervaded. (24)
Residing in the heart, it vibrates as the sound (nāda), and all the vital airs, beginning with prāṇa, [reside there].
It is indeed the agent in all activities, whether they be collective or individual.
He is indeed to be known as the creator; therefore, O Guha, you have not attained him.
Whatever activities there may be, beginning with creation and ending with destruction, [all belong to Him]. (26)
He is indeed the creator of all, the eternally manifest Supreme Brahman;
the twenty-four principles [constitute nature], while the Puruṣa is the twenty-fifth.
For he is indeed the creator of all those various things;

(p. 38a) "Everything has been known by me, everything has been heard by me, yet, O Father, that which pertains to the Kaula tradition as it resides in the mouths of the *khecarīs* has not [been heard]. (1)
"O child, this which you have requested as a question is great knowledge and indeed great discernment— the Kaula tradition that is the domain of the sky-farers."
Out of affection for my son, I shall tell you a secret that is like a marvel;
for indeed, O Guha, they attain success through him by means of his splendor.
But for ordinary mortals whose minds are afflicted by the world and who have fallen into false conceptualizations, O dear child, truth indeed does not succeed.
That which is called the life-force (jīva), the immortal nectar situated within the space of the heart—
those who possess form drink it by resorting to the central channel.
Having drunk that, they attain satisfaction; for this reason, indeed, they drink it. Established within the channels of the lineage, they satisfy the gods and the ancestors.
O Guha, their liberation has been declared by Śiva through this method,
and not by means of fire-offerings, oblations, or sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
The Rūpikas devour my flesh, bones, blood, and marrow;
for the nectar, O child, is the supreme state situated within the heart.
But their success does not come at all unless they have gratified Bhairava;
for them, Bhairava is gratified through the sprinkling of the sacrificial animal (paśu) upon the dharma.
The power of consciousness (cicchakti) resides within the hearts of those bound souls (paśus);
and liberation is always established in the sacrifice taught by Bhairava.
But that [sacrifice] should be known as "concealed" (pihita); otherwise, indeed, speak thus:
"O child, if animals should kill [the victim] according to this procedure. (11)
Liberation is said to occur together with the liberation of the sacrificial animal;
thus, the great ones achieve perfection endowed with the eight Siddhis. (12)
O wielder of power, what distinction is there among common accomplishments?
To whom is this knowledge known—a knowledge equal to supreme realization, consisting of both the object of knowledge and its comprehension? (13)
Brahmā and the others are his cattle; what need is there to mention other cattle?
And Prajāpati is the original creator of all cattle. (14)
Since that very [being] has been consecrated by sprinkling, it therefore becomes superior to the Kaulas;
for among the Vedic sacrifices, O best of Brahmins, they slaughter animals. (15)
In all the Bhairava systems, practitioners slay the male sacrificial animal (puṃpaśu),
which is the subtle body (sūkṣmapuryaṣṭaka) residing within the hearts of living beings.
The Yoginīs kill that sacrificial animal; having killed it, they attain success among the Siddhis.
When the vital breaths (prāṇa and apāna) arise therein, they have gone to dissolution in Bindu and Nāda. || 17 ||
O Śikhidhvaja, those Rūpikās drink [the blood] after having slaughtered the animal;
for this is their destination, and they indeed obtain that as their own self.
That which is the space within the living soul, situated in the hearts of all beings, they indeed drink [the vital essence] without knowing it, through the flow of the prāṇa and apāna breaths. (19)
[He is] indeed the one who immediately removes the fear of poverty and is the liberator;

by means of which [practice], according to the rite of Bhairava, they drink for the sake of accomplishment, through the power of yoga correctly performed according to the procedure taught by Bhairava. || 21 ||
O Guha, he who drinks liquor openly as if it were milk is a perfected one (siddha) and a true practitioner (sādhaka); all others are indeed considered mediocre.
He who, having obtained this [mantra] with merely a flower, offers it to many, provides milk as the essence when a crisis has arisen. (23)
O child, that perfected one, Kṛṣṇa, is always white-handed Guha;
he moves within the interval between prāṇa and apāna, traveling through the three channels.
Drinking that divine nectar, which is supreme and bestows the highest siddhi, one likewise abandons the solar path as well as the lunar path. (25)
Those who drink the supreme nectar of him who has entered the path of Brahman.
O Lord, if you are pleased, speak that which is desired, true, and beneficial, by the mere understanding of which delusive cognition ceases. (1)
Listen, my child, O best among all the wise, to what is right;
I shall answer without doubt the question that you have asked. (2)
That power which is supreme and subtle, unmanifest, and whose purpose is Śiva,
which resides within all beings and by which the entire universe is upheld.
O Guha, the Śakti, empowered by the command of Śiva, devours and creates the entire creation of beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, including all that is moving and unmoving.
"Furthermore, O Śikhidhvaja, it is the truth, the absolute truth, that we have no power [to do so] against Brahmā, Viṣṇu, nor even the Fire-god. (5)
All the deities, beginning with Indra, and the great sages, beginning with Satva,
are born again and again, and they die again and again.
Furthermore, the withdrawal of power never occurs here;
for that power, which abides in supreme non-duality, is indeed never lost.
That subtle [power] is eternally risen, originating from the nectar of Śiva;
by her this entire universe, the creation of beings consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is pervaded.
But she, O child, is internalized and resides within the hearts of all;
just as piercers [of gems] act by depending upon each individual gem.
In that same way, O Guha, the great elements are awakened by the awakening of their power;
Śiva is directly the thread of them, and by him they are strung together.
By these, the entire universe is pervaded, as far as the range of the cosmic egg;
all the great elements are produced from the power of consciousness. (11)
The power of consciousness (cic-chakti), born from Śiva, remains unmanifest and pervades all things;
indeed, the deluded, utterly bewildered by the Great Illusion (mahāmāyā), do not know it. 12.
There is no being whatsoever in whom she does not reside;
she dwells everywhere in the form of fire, supported by the wind.
Those whose stainless wisdom is that of the Sage behold the welfare of all;
their body becomes the abode of Brahman, and therein wisdom itself is the lamp.
Having kindled it, they behold whatever is within the house;
having seen that, they shall go to the unborn, imperishable state.
O Śikhidhvaja, she is unborn, stainless, subtle, eternally risen, and perfectly pure; she resides within all beings, beginning with Brahmā.
"O Śikhidhvaja, those by whom [this] is known are indeed liberated; those who perceive it otherwise are bound. Together with Brahmā and the others, we ourselves are certainly not liberated. (17)
Then indeed all other yogins, intent on meditation and devoted to it, entered into meditative absorption, desiring to follow the path of the Mākṣas. || 18 ||
O Guha, they worship with various sacrifices that which has arisen from within Him;
for there is indeed one single cause therein, though the application of means is diverse and distinct.
For those in whom yoga is indeed characterized by sattva, liberation will certainly occur;
for those desiring heaven it is characterized by rajas, and for those enveloped by tamas it leads to hell.
O child, when that sacrifice is performed by them with sattvic qualities, they then go to liberation; when it is performed by humans with rajasic qualities, it yields the fruit of attaining heaven.
The *tāmasa* [sacrifice] is performed by those born as animals, by the deluded, the ignorant, and the unlearned;
therefore, with every effort, one should undertake the *sāttvika* sacrifice.
O child, the rājasa and tāmasa [types of sacrifice] lead to rebirth;
however, in the sāttvika mental sacrifice, no violence is found. (23)
O child, both the rājasa and tāmasa [forms of sacrifice] are preceded by violence;
those who worship Sadāśiva through mental sacrifice alone do not [engage in such violence].
They are liberated from all sins; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O you who worship the Truth!
For those in whom the purification of material substances is performed, that constitutes the supreme provision.
Examine that with effort, O Six-faced One; if it proves to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika), then that collection of materials becomes pure.
For when impure material, characterized by passion (rājasa) and ignorance (tāmasa), is offered at all times, it becomes,
through that [offering], stainless and is instead regarded as if it were mere grass.
There is no substance in the three worlds that is always characterized by sattva;
therefore, those who always sacrifice with wealth are not liberated.
Alternatively, if one should somehow obtain an object that is pure (sāttvika),
it should be given to a deity, a guru, or to a Brahmin who is a proponent of the Veda.
And that which is proclaimed as infinite, incalculable, and even in the slightest measure, becomes inexhaustible, my child, even for hundreds of millions of eons. (30)
One should never employ that substance for the purpose of ritual requisites;
whatever external requisites there may be, they all originate from the power of consciousness (cicchakti). || 31 ||
Since harm would come to them from that [action], one should therefore avoid it;
for they are all living beings, and Śiva resides in their hearts.
The flowers are indeed endowed with life, the fruits are endowed with life,
and all species of trees are to be known as having living animals within them.

Having abandoned that [worldly path], you alone perform sacrifice, possessing the perfection of the fruit of the scriptures; while those who remain intent on rewards are occupied with subjugation, attraction, and killing.
They sacrifice with those very living beings, O child, which have arisen from the power of consciousness—the fourteen-fold creation of beings, both moving and unmoving. (35)
Everything is produced from the power of consciousness; by killing it, one is certainly not liberated.
The arising of power and the determination of the purification of substances have been understood by me through your command;
now I desire to hear about the desired [deity] and the supreme answer regarding the worshiper. (1)
I have performed severe penance for many ages and kalpas;
then the Blessed Lord Śiva, the supreme destroyer of misfortune, was pleased.
"O Vadame, today I am pleased with you, O Umāpati;
[the vow is] non-violence toward all beings, both moving and unmoving. (3)
For this indeed is the nectar, O child, the imperishable and the eternal; one should know that [other] syllables are characterized by violence, and therefore one should avoid them. || 4 ||
Therefore, O child, those who sacrifice for this purpose— the human sacrifice which is imperishable and immortal— attain what is beneficial and are liberated from the bonds of existence.
O Śikhidhvaja, we did not speak thus out of a desire for enjoyments;
rather, it was due to ignorance regarding the instruction, being excluded from the knowledge of Śiva.
Then, the reality that is known as the support for the path to liberation—
the supreme reality free from conceptual proliferation, as well as the lower and the intermediate— [was revealed].
The supreme Śakti is free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañcā), and the supreme Śiva is free from conceptual proliferation;
one should perform his sacrifice, for it is indeed free from conceptual proliferation.
Bathing, meditation, worship, recitation, and fifthly, fire-offering—
these should be performed with the mind according to the rite prescribed by the rules.
Thus [ends] the glorious [work].
O Lord, you have previously described mental bathing and other rites;
I wish to hear about that as it truly is, so please explain it to me.
The Śivatīrtha situated within the body is more beneficial than all other holy places;
it is likewise so in the world of Bhūr, the world of Bhuvar, and the world of Svar.
O Guha, all rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā and all oceans beginning with the Kṣīroda reside right there in Mānasa; indeed, everything is present there.
The mental sacred ford (mānasa-tīrtha) is indeed Śiva; situated in the center of the lotus of the heart, O child, is that auspicious confluence consisting of the nature of sound (nāda).
The dense thicket of Agni and Soma, with the prāṇa and apāna as its reservoirs,
has its current situated within the channel of the Suṣumṇā at that sacred ford.
(44b) And being bathed on all sides by the flood of nectar from the Fourth state,
no obstacles here— whether they be the wicked among the moving or the unmoving— can cause harm.
Then, the auspicious bath there at Śivatīrtha and in the Mānasa lake was performed;
indeed, no violence was seen here, nor was any tax collected.
Whatever beings there are in this world, whether moving or stationary, and whatever sacred shrines there may be— they all abide as if within it, for the sake of the cause of self-purification.
All external holy places are indeed constructed by conceptualization; they abide within the mental holy place of Śiva, which removes all that is inauspicious.
Those who have conceived external holy fords and shrines are always tormented by obstacles residing in the heavens, on earth, and in the intermediate space.
Therefore, O child, they have been defiled by someone at Śivatīrtha; for that reason, O Guha, external holy sites have always been avoided.
In the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), there is indeed the destruction of obstacles;
since harm would come to them [the practitioners], one should therefore avoid those [obstacles]. || 12 ||
Stainless, free from obstacles, bestowing wisdom, and destroying sin,
it constantly flows with nectar situated within the Piṅgalā.
The Suṣumṇā is blissful and profound, while Turyā has the ultimate as its range;
it is the stainless attainment of the true nature, that bliss which is cool with joy.
Having attained that auspicious sacred ford (śivatīrtha) which indeed resides within one's own heart,
one should always perform ablutions therein according to the ritual prescribed by the rules.
One should perform the salutation at twilight there and offer libations to the ancestors and the deities;
whatever else is to be done, perform all of that mentally.
Alternatively, whatever sacred site (tīrtha) is desired by the mind is remembered;
all of them reside right here, dedicated to non-violence (ahiṃsā). || 17 ||
Together with Brahmā and the other gods, we have attained this through the use of the water from Śiva’s sacred bathing-place;
for this is indeed the supreme sacred site, and this is indeed the supreme recitation. (18)
For this indeed is the supreme bath; O Guha, one should truly bathe there. External holy sites and all external mantras are satisfied in every way.
The mantras are pleased when one is joyful; otherwise, they are like mere water.
O Guha, whatever living beings, including the poor and others, reside at sacred fords (tīrthas), [they too are affected].
Therefore, those who are devoid of consciousness abandon their objects through the thorough knowledge of the sacred ford of Śiva and by the power of perfect yoga.
The practitioner, being well-composed, is constantly purified by that;
for herein no one is harmed, nor are sesame seeds or *darbha* grasses destroyed.
But whether it be silver or gold, or even the falling of a sword,
nothing at all is lost through the remembrance of Śivatīrtha.
I have learned of Śivatīrtha in that place as it was described;
now I desire to further understand the meditation whose nature is the Lord of the Body. (1)
I have revealed to you all direct knowledge;
now I shall show you both the perceptible and the imperceptible.
O child, by those who perceive the Self and have fully understood the Śivatīrtha, everything pertaining to the path of liberation is attained; of this there is no doubt.
Those who are established in the knowledge of the Self— those who know the Self and perceive the Self— are always pure, my child, regardless of which stage of life (āśrama) they occupy.
For them, there is indeed no need for purification by bathing, nor is there any use for mantras;
he alone is the auspicious mantra, the scripture, and the supreme sacred field.
Indeed, no obstacles whatsoever in the three worlds can harm him;
by his mere sight, they perish and flee in the ten directions.
Neither the cardinal directions nor the intermediate directions, nor mudrās nor seats—
these one should perceive through the instrument [of practice] by means of the power of perfect yoga.

One should practice inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka) as the third; having applied these according to their true nature, one should then commence meditation (dhyāna). || 8 ||
O child, free from doubt, one should perceive it through meditation;
examine that with effort, situated within the interior of the wheel of channels (nāḍicakra).
O Six-faced One, that [body] has seventy-two thousand channels;
each one indeed revolves, situated between the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
Of all the winds, however, the prāṇa and apāna are the impellers.
Among them, the prāṇa is their life-force; having bowed to that prāṇa, they know it as supreme. (11)
Therefore, O Six-faced One, one should indeed perceive that entire wheel of channels; Piṅgalā becomes the navel of that wheel.
That Praṇava becomes the wheel, and Piṅgalā is indeed its crest;
by knowing that, O child, one beholds Śiva, the supreme cause. (13)
O Guha, having kindled the lamp of knowledge and meditated with the fire of wisdom,
one then reaches the God who stands situated within the interior of the *piṅgalā*.
That cave of the heart is to be known as the pericarp in the center of the heart;
he who beholds the God situated in its center truly beholds. || 15 ||
Situated in the midst of the sun, moon, and fire, it is free from impurity and devoid of any mark;
it has the form of a *kadamba* flower bud and possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Resembling the fire at the end of an eon and difficult to behold for those who have not disciplined themselves, his inference is indeed not perceived through any logical reason whatsoever. (17)
Having thus meditated upon that deity residing within the cave of the heart,
one should then proceed with mental effort toward the human [abode].
I have understood meditation, the object of meditation, and that which is to be known;
now, O Lord of the Secret Heart, I wish to hear about worship. (1)
O Śikhivāhana, those secrets which were spoken at the beginning—
this secret has been revealed by you today, which has not been told to anyone else.

Those who are ignorant and those who do not know the self, as well as those who are wise—consciousness is established in all beings by its nature as pure awareness (*citsvabhāva*). Since it is that which makes beings sentient, it would indeed delude them. (4)
O child, one attains the power of consciousness; auspicious and inauspicious pleasure and pain are seen as the very self of Śiva, established everywhere in its manifested form.
The Supreme Power experiences both the impure and the pure, as well as pleasure and pain; yet that which is supreme here remains untainted.
And that [non-violence], O child, is the witness for both sides;
knowing this, one should indeed practice non-violence toward all beings.
Therefore, those seeking liberation should perform a mental sacrifice,
rather than one involving violence, excessive ritual apparatus, and [worldly] yoga.
For those who perform sacrifices while bound by desire, heaven is their reward;
however, through yoga that is free from the notion of "I," there is always an absence of violence.
Having returned again and again, it repeatedly goes to destruction.
Knowing this, one should perform every supreme human sacrifice. (10)
He who perceives the omnipresent being as equal in all—just as it is in himself, so too in others—that is indeed declared to be non-violence (ahiṃsā). 11.
O Guha, he who perceives the same in himself as in others is liberated from the bondage of primordial nature (prakṛti) and abides in the eternal Śiva. 12.
For this sattvic state is indeed described by Śiva as mental;
it consists of the internal ear and so forth, O child, as has been declared by me in the Darśana.
For they indeed harm the elements; therefore, that [purification] preceded by non-violence is the cause for the internal arrangement of the mind intended for the purification of the elements.
O child, it is performed in every respect through ritual action as seen in the scriptures;
having first performed the purification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and likewise the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), O child.
Then that practitioner becomes fit for the worship of Śiva;
moreover, O dear one, he who knows the Self shall be eternally pure at all times. (16)
For him there is neither purity nor impurity, since his abode is that which is to be purified;
being eternally established in purity, he accomplishes nothing at all.
O child, that [reality] is impure in its true nature due to the stains of conceptualized objects;
yet he whose power is fierce is indeed the supreme one who purifies it.
He purifies all beings and uplifts them;
therefore, O child, for one who knows the Self, the ritual emblem (ketana) is purposeless.
He alone is truly possessed of enjoyment, for Śiva is the supreme cause;
he alone is the supreme gift, and therein all his impurities are purified.
By means of the self through the self, he worships the Supreme Lord according to the prescribed rule and by the power of perfect yoga.
He performs a mental sacrifice with his mind toward the Lord; all the deities, beginning with Brahmā, as well as the great seers, likewise worship Him mentally. (22)
O Śikhivāhana, that present [sacrifice] was never performed by me through a mental rite;
for the sake of yoga, the collection of materials remains right here. (23)
Now, O Śikhidhvaja, whatever desire you seek in your mind that is wished for by the mind, you shall indeed obtain all of that which is mental.
Whether one worships with form or again without form, both of these, my child, worship at the same time; perform whichever pleases you.

That which is without characteristics and devoid of intrinsic nature—that very object, in the form of an image—is fashioned with mental activity possessing form by means of the mind whose nature is consciousness. (26)
And no conscious being whatsoever can exist without a nature that is unchanging;
therefore, my child, you should always worship that which eternally abides as power (śakti).
The notion of consciousness arises from consciousness and is established among both the real and the unreal. || 28 ||
The principles (tattvas), elements (bhūtas), and states of being (bhāvas) abide within by means of the power of consciousness (cicchakti);
they are established in the principle of Śiva (ciattattva), while the all-pervading Lord is omnipresent like the essence of mercury.
O child, all this beneficial advice has been made manifest within your heart;
therefore, worship Him with diligence through the rites prescribed by the sacred injunctions.
O child, there is no one to whom that [Ahimsā] does not abide in the heart;
therefore, O child, one should worship it with the auspicious flowers of non-violence.
Furthermore, O child, one should worship that which resides in the heart with all desired objects;
indeed, all the gifts that have been described in the Śivadharmas [should be offered]. 32.
O Śikhivāhana, all those [offerings] when given become the fulfillment of all desires; likewise, the Mānasa sacrifice is supreme.
This sacrifice is indeed supreme, the most excellent among all sacrifices.
He who worships with the *iḍā* and other [oblations] is said to perform a *rājasa* sacrifice. (34)
The Suṣumṇā is to be known as the enjoyment of tamas, while [enjoyment] in the rising of Piṅgalā is sāttvika.
Having abandoned you in the Suṣumṇā, one should worship that which resides in the Piṅgalā channel. (35)
One should investigate that with effort; it is called the Brahmā-nāḍī.
One should worship that deity situated in its center, and not this [other]. || 36 ||
Whatever is to be done, all that occurs during the rising of Piṅgalā; indeed, all things arise from the Fourth State (turya) and have entered the locus of the Fourth. || 37 ||
One should contemplate all desires, for otherwise they lead to harm;
having brought them to dissolution in the fourth state, one should always worship that which resides in the heart. 38.
How can one worship that which resides in the heart if one has no access to the Fourth State (turya)?
But he who knows both—that which resides in the heart and that which is established in the Fourth—in accordance with reality, [he truly knows]. (39)
O Śikhivāhana, he ought to perform worship of these [deities] primarily as one, by means of Śiva who resides within the prāṇa and apāna breaths. (40)
The practitioner should join them, O dear one; he is indeed called a practitioner.
Prāṇa and apāna are intertwined, endowed with rajas and tamas. (41)
Therefore, my child, one should always avoid those two at the time of sacrifice;
instead, one should perform the worship of Śiva through association with those who are characterized by sattva.
Indeed, your worship of the Fire has not been performed otherwise;
for the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, [are contained therein]. (43)
Through the sprinkling of flowers of non-violence, that [Lord] shall always be worshipped;
O All-pervading One, by means of the mental sacrifice, I am forever liberated. (44)
Nevertheless, I truly desire to know the supreme mantra for constant recitation. || 1 ||

O Śikhidhvaja, with mental recitations and floods of syllables, one should perform the secret and most esoteric muttering, the supreme among all forms of japa, directed toward the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
Many kinds of recitation have been proclaimed by Śiva, the Supreme Self;
yet it is mental recitation that bestows the fruit of the path to liberation. (3)
This path has been revealed by my Lord, who is pleased with me;
therefore, O son of Kṛttikā, I shall now declare the secret.
That supreme state which resides in the heart of all beings—he indeed counts it as the object of recitation; he truly performs the recitation.
Those devoid of knowledge and realization do not understand at all;
O child, such a person performs the recitation of mantras day after day. (6)

O Guha, they say that within it, by means of supreme and auspicious jewels in an uninterrupted succession, the power of consciousness (cicchakti) of the Sun is manifested; thus has it been described to you.
Indeed, this rosary is the supreme [tool] for yogins who contemplate reality;
it belongs to those established in the attainment of results such as subjugation, attraction, and killing.
O child, for those who know the Self, there is no further need for the recitation of mantras with rosaries many times over, nor for the systems of mantra and tantra.
For them, the sole purpose would be the knowledge of the Self;
having known that, O Mahāsena, O Guha, one should abandon the mantras and tantras.
Alternatively, O Guha, there is no need for a specific count in this mental recitation;
therefore, I shall explain how it should be performed—listen to that.

Śiva constantly performs the recitation (*japya*) within a single day and night, numbering six thousand times [and] six hundred times. This indeed becomes the recitation of Śiva, for Śiva brings auspiciousness even to one who acts inauspiciously. (14)
The prāṇa draws in the apāna, and the apāna likewise draws in the prāṇa;
he who draws both of them together performs the japa, O Guha. (15)
From the heart-center to the limit of twelve (dvādaśānta), and from the limit of twelve back to the heart—
this coming and going is to be known as that eternal Brahman-japa.
The mental recitation, as well as the recitation with a rosary, and the fire-ritual are already known; O Lord, please explain the true nature of the funeral rites.
O child, out of affection for you, I have revealed this nectar of my commands;
I shall further explain the mental fire-sacrifice (agnikārya). || 2 ||
O Śikhivāhana, all beings, both moving and unmoving, being deluded, do not know the supreme splendor residing within their own hearts. (3)
The sun blazes; by its splendor, O Guha, that very splendor of the fire and likewise of the moon is filled. || 4 ||
Therefore, O Śikhivāhana, one should worship the fires according to the prescribed rules;
for the Guhyakas and other spirits devour the sacrificial oblation offered into external fires.
If there are defects in the mantra and defects in the ritual, or if it is performed with impure instruments,
then, my child, that offering sacrificed in external fires is lost.
Since all the materials for the sacrificial equipment, such as the fuel-wood and so forth, originate from the power of consciousness (cicchakti),
and since these are offered here [in the sacrifice], they are therefore preceded by violence.
O child, the worship of the internal fire within one's own body is preceded by non-violence;
this is the Śiva-fire, which is majestic and brings about auspiciousness while removing inauspiciousness.
There is no need there for the purificatory rites beginning with the conception (*garbhādāna*); for is a vessel not made by you without the use of girdles or a womb? (9)
O Garuḍa-vehicled One, this must indeed be performed here according to the rule:
three sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are situated within the body, as are the three fires.
O child, the Gārhapatya fire is in the heart-pit, the Dakṣiṇa fire is in the navel-pit, and that which resides in the mouth-pit is known by the name Āhavanīya.
O child, I have shown you to you in due order the triad of fire-pits;
one should perform the oblation for them according to the ritual procedure seen in the scriptures.
Resorting to the suṣumṇā channel, one should indeed perform the northern course (uttarāyaṇa);
then, O Guha, one should offer oblations into the southern fire situated in the pit of the navel.
Having caused the arising of the iḍā channel, one should indeed perform the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana);
then, O Guha, the Āhavanīya fire is situated in the mouth-cavity.
The Gārhapatya fire, which always resides within the sacrificial pit of the heart—in that one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) by means of the equinoxal rite (viṣuvatkaraṇa). || 15 ||
O child, the equinox occurs with the rising of the Piṅga-nāḍī;
whatever one worships at that time shall all become inexhaustible. || 16 ||
All desires and whatever is intended by the mind are accomplished;
one should offer the five vital winds, beginning with prāṇa, into the fire in their proper sequence. || 17 ||
By those oblations offered, the entire universe becomes completely satiated;
it becomes nectar, O child, and that nectar remains.
Then that entire universe becomes satisfied for others as well,
O Lord of Peacocks, by those who have known that which resides within the interval between the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
They too have vomited forth the divine, supreme nectar arising from the state of Turiya;
one should constantly worship the fire with the clarified butter of that nectar born of Turiya.
This worship of Agni is inexhaustible, auspicious, and bestows liberation.
Thus ends the [work] concerning the fire of the venerable Brahmasandhāna, [composed by] Jācāniyo.
Today my intellect has borne fruit, having heard of the supreme state of Brahman.
